items.title: Necessity: -malı / -meli
items.goal: Say what has to be done, give strong advice and reproach a past failure.

blocks.text: -malı / -meli expresses necessity, moral obligation or strong advice. Add the suffix to the stem, then the person marker: git-meli-yim (I must go), gel-meli-sin (you must come), oku-malı-yız (we must read).

The negative is formed with -ma / -me: gitmemeliyim (I must not go), gelmemelisin (you must not come). In the past: gitmeliydim (I should have gone), gelmeliydi (he should have come). The suffix -ydi adds a reproach or a regret.

-malı is often an inner obligation or a piece of advice: Daha dikkatli olmalısın. (You should be more careful.) For an obligation imposed from outside, -mak zorunda is preferred: Her gün işe gitmek zorundayım. (I have to go to work every day.)

items.fr: I must get up early tomorrow.
You should read this book.
You must not smoke here.
He should have been more careful.

blocks.text: To ask for an opinion: <tur>Gitmeli miyim?</tur> (Should I go?), <tur>Ona söylemeli miyim?</tur> (Should I tell him?). The particle <tur>mi</tur> comes after the conjugated verb.

quiz.q: How do you say « I must leave » with gitmek?
quiz.why: The first person of -malı is -yim: git + meli + yim = gitmeliyim.
The negative -me comes before -meli: git-me-meli-sin = you must not go.

items.title: Obligation: -mak zorunda
items.goal: Express an external constraint, say « I have to » and tell obligation apart from prohibition.

blocks.text: The structure -mak / -mek zorunda means « to have to ». The verb stays in the infinitive and the person is marked on zorunda: gitmek zorundayım (I have to go), gelmek zorundasın (you have to come).

<tur>Gitmek zorunda değilim.</tur> means « I don't have to go », not « I must not go ». For a prohibition, use <tur>gitmemeliyim</tur> (I must not go) or <tur>gitmek yasak</tur> (going there is forbidden).

<tur>zorunda</tur> can be conjugated in the past or the future: <tur>Dün çalışmak zorundaydım.</tur> (Yesterday I had to work.) <tur>Yarın erken kalkmak zorunda olacağım.</tur> (Tomorrow I will have to get up early.)

items.fr: I have to go to work every day.

items.tr: Yarın sınav var, erken kalkmak zorundayım.
items.fr: There is an exam tomorrow, I have to get up early.
Today I don't have to work.
He was forced to do that.

blocks.text: -malı = personal obligation, advice, moral duty. zorunda = external constraint: a rule, a timetable, a situation. Sigara içmemelisin. (You shouldn't smoke.) Burada sigara içmek yasak. (Smoking is forbidden here.)

quiz.q: How do you say « I have to work »?
quiz.why: An external constraint is expressed with -mak zorunda: çalışmak zorundayım.

quiz.q: What does « Gitmek zorunda değilim » mean?
quiz.why: zorunda değil expresses the absence of obligation, not a prohibition.

items.title: The past perfect: -mıştı
items.goal: Tell of an action completed before another past action.

blocks.text: -mıştı / -mişti / -muştu / -müştü expresses a past completed before another moment in the past: « I had already done ». Add -mış to the stem, then -tı / -ti, then the person marker: gel-miş-ti-m (I had come).

blocks.caption: The past perfect of gelmek and okumak
head: Person
gelmek (to come)
okumak (to read)

blocks.text: It is used with time markers such as <tur>daha önce</tur> (before), <tur>önceden</tur> (previously), <tur>çoktan</tur> (already, long ago) or a time clause: <tur>Dün geldiğinde biz çoktan yemek yemiştik.</tur> (When he arrived yesterday, we had already eaten.)

<tur>Geldim</tur> = I came (simple past). <tur>Gelmiştim</tur> = I had come (past perfect). The second places the action before another past action. <tur>Gelmişim</tur> = apparently I came / I apparently did the action (evidential, another use of -miş).

items.fr: I had read the book before going there.

items.tr: Dün geldiğinde biz çoktan yemek yemiştik.
items.fr: When you arrived yesterday, we had already eaten.
I had never spoken Turkish before.
He had prepared for the exam, but he got nervous.

blocks.text: The past perfect is very common in stories and explanations: it sets the scene before the main event. You will often find it with <tur>çoktan</tur>, <tur>zaten</tur> (already) and <tur>henüz</tur> (not yet).

vocab: to get nervous, to get excited

quiz.why: -mıştı expresses a past completed before another past moment: I had read.

quiz.q: Which form means « they had already left »?
quiz.why: The third person plural of -mıştı is -mışlardı: gitmişlerdi.

items.title: The future in the past: -(y)acaktı
items.goal: Say « I was going to leave », « he was supposed to come »: a past plan that never happened.

blocks.text: -acaktı / -ecekti expresses a future seen from the past: « I was going to do », « I was about to do », often with the idea that the plan did not happen. Add -acak / -ecek, then the past marker -tı / -ti and the person.

This form is very useful for explaining a change of plan: <tur>Dün size gelecektim ama işim çıktı.</tur> (I was going to come to your place yesterday, but something came up.) <tur>Sınavdan sonra tatile gidecektik, ama iptal oldu.</tur> (We were going to go on holiday after the exam, but it was cancelled.)

<tur>Gelecektim</tur> can simply mean « I was going to come » without stressing the failure. But with <tur>ama</tur>, <tur>fakat</tur> or <tur>ancak</tur>, it is understood that the plan was interrupted. <tur>Gelecektim ama gelemedim.</tur> = I was going to come, but I couldn't.

The question <tur>Ne yapacaktın?</tur> means « What were you going to do? ». <tur>Ne zaman gelecektin?</tur> = « When were you supposed to come? ». The negative: <tur>gelmeyecektim</tur> (I was not going to come), <tur>gitmeyecektik</tur> (we were not going to go).

items.tr: Dün size gelecektim ama işim çıktı.
items.fr: I was going to come to your place yesterday, but something came up.

items.tr: Sınavdan sonra tatile gidecektik, ama iptal oldu.
items.fr: We were going to go on holiday after the exam, but it was cancelled.
He was going to come too, but he fell ill.
What were you going to do?

blocks.tag: Simple future or future in the past?
blocks.text: <tur>Yarın geleceğim.</tur> = I will come tomorrow (simple future). <tur>Dün gelecektim.</tur> = I was going to come yesterday (future in the past). The time marker and the context make all the difference.

options: I was going to come yesterday
quiz.why: -acaktı places a future seen from the past: I was going to come yesterday.

quiz.q: What is the negative form of « I was going to come »?
quiz.why: The negative of the future in the past is -meyecektim: gelmeyecektim.

items.title: Advanced conjunctions
items.goal: Nuance an argument with « however », « whereas », « otherwise », « moreover ».

blocks.text: <tur>Halbuki</tur> and <tur>oysa</tur> introduce a contrast: <tur>Çok çalıştı, halbuki hiç hazır değildi.</tur> (He worked hard, whereas he was not ready at all.) <tur>Meğer</tur> marks a revelation: <tur>Meğer anahtarı masada bırakmışım.</tur> (It turns out I had left the key on the table.)

<tur>Yoksa</tur> and <tur>aksi halde</tur> introduce an alternative or an unfortunate consequence: <tur>Erken çık, yoksa otobüsü kaçıracaksın.</tur> (Leave early, otherwise you will miss the bus.) <tur>Aksi halde</tur> is more formal: <tur>Ödevini yap, aksi halde notun düşer.</tur>

<tur>Üstelik</tur>, <tur>hatta</tur> and <tur>hem de</tur> add information that reinforces the statement: <tur>Üstelik çok da pahalı.</tur> (What's more, it is very expensive.) <tur>Hatta onu ben de gördüm.</tur> (Even I saw it.) <tur>Hem de ne kadar güzel!</tur> (And what's more, how beautiful it is!)

items.fr: He worked hard, but despite that he did not succeed.
Leave early, otherwise you will miss the bus.

items.tr: Oysa ben onu çok iyi tanıyordum.
items.fr: Whereas I knew him very well.
It turns out I had left the key on the table.

blocks.text: <tur>Ama</tur> is the everyday « but ». <tur>Ancak</tur>, <tur>fakat</tur> and <tur>lakin</tur> are more formal. <tur>Halbuki</tur> and <tur>oysa</tur> suit argumentative writing; in speech, <tur>ama</tur> and <tur>yoksa</tur> are also heard.

quiz.why: yoksa introduces an alternative or an unfortunate consequence: otherwise.
meğer reveals information discovered after the event: it turns out that.

items.title: Advanced participles
items.goal: Build rich noun phrases with -an, -dık, -acak and -mış.

blocks.text: Participles turn a clause into an adjective. -an / -en refers to the one who does: çalışan insan (the person who works). -dık / -dik refers to what has been done or to the object of the action: çalıştığım şirket (the company where I work). -acak / -ecek projects into the future: gideceğim yer (the place where I will go).

blocks.caption: Four participles of okumak (to read)
head: Form
Meaning
Example
rows: that I have read / where I read

blocks.text: The participle -dık always takes a possessive suffix that indicates the agent: okuduğum (that I have read), okuduğun (that you have read), okuduğu (that he has read), okuduğumuz (that we have read). The -an participle, by contrast, takes none: okuyan öğrenci.

The participle -mış / -miş describes a state resulting from an action: kırılmış cam (broken glass), pişmiş yemek (cooked food), donmuş göl (frozen lake). Do not confuse it with the evidential past gelmiş (« apparently he came »).

items.fr: The people who work here are very kind.
I forgot the title of the book I read.
We are going to the exhibition that opens tomorrow.
We replaced the broken glass.

blocks.text: Turkish stacks participles before the noun: <tur>dün okuduğum yeni Türkçe kitabın adı</tur> (the title of the new Turkish book I read yesterday). Each participle keeps its place, from the most general to the most precise.

quiz.why: -dığ + the possessive suffix -ım expresses « where I work ».

quiz.q: Which participle describes a state resulting from an action?
quiz.why: -mış forms stative participles: kırılmış cam (broken glass).

items.title: Duration and limit: -dığı sürece, -dıkça
items.goal: Say « as long as », « the more… the more… », « before » and « after ».

blocks.text: -dığı sürece means « as long as »: çalıştığın sürece (as long as you work), ben burada olduğum sürece (as long as I am here). The possessive suffix of -dığı agrees with the subject of the clause.
-dıkça expresses « as… » or « the more… the more… »: çalıştıkça (as you work), okudukça (the more you read), öğrendikçe (as I learn), geldikçe (each time I come).

blocks.caption: The useful forms
head: Structure
Example
Meaning
rows: As long as your health is good, you can work.
The more I learn Turkish, the more I like it.
Let me know before you leave.

blocks.text: <tur>-madan</tur> on its own means « without »: <tur>Kahve içmeden çalışamam.</tur> (I can't work without drinking coffee.) With <tur>önce</tur>, it takes the meaning « before »: <tur>Gitmeden önce haber ver.</tur> (Let me know before you leave.) Conversely, <tur>-dıktan sonra</tur> = « after ».

These structures are very common in writing and in instructions. <tur>Ders çalışmadan önce telefonunu kapat.</tur> (Turn off your phone before studying.) <tur>Spor yaptıkça kendini daha iyi hissediyorsun.</tur> (The more you exercise, the better you feel.)

items.fr: As long as your health is good, you can work.
The more I learn Turkish, the more I like it.
Let me know before you leave.
Take the medicine after eating.

blocks.text: <tur>Sürece</tur> comes from <tur>sürmek</tur> (to last). <tur>olduğu sürece</tur> can also be used with an adjective: <tur>Hava güzel olduğu sürece yürüyebiliriz.</tur> (As long as the weather is nice, we can walk.)

quiz.why: -dıkça expresses gradual progression: as you work, little by little.

quiz.q: How do you say « before leaving »?

items.title: The past conditional
items.goal: Express regret or an unreal hypothesis: « if I had known… », « I should have… ».

blocks.text: The past conditional is formed with -seydi / -saydı: gelseydim (if I had come), yapsaydım (if I had done), olsaydı (if it had been). The vowel follows vowel harmony.

blocks.caption: The past conditional of gelmek and yapmak
head: Person
gelmek (to come)
yapmak (to do)

blocks.text: The consequence is often in the future in the past or in the conditional: <tur>Gelseydin, onu görürdün.</tur> (If you had come, you would have seen him.) <tur>Daha çok çalışsaydım, sınavı kazanacaktım.</tur> (If I had studied more, I would have passed the exam.)

<tur>Keşke</tur> means « if only ». It combines with the past conditional: <tur>Keşke daha erken başlasaydım.</tur> (If only I had started earlier.) <tur>Keşke gelmeseydim.</tur> (If only I had not come.)

<tur>-miş olsaydım</tur> can also be used: <tur>Daha çok çalışmış olsaydım, kazanırdım.</tur> (If I had worked more, I would have won.) This variant stresses the completed action. The meaning stays close to <tur>-seydim</tur>.

items.fr: If you had come, you would have seen him.
If I had studied more, I would have passed the exam.
If only I had started earlier.
If the weather had been nice, we would have gone for a walk.

blocks.text: Gelseydin = if you had come (unreal hypothesis about the past). Gelsen = if you came (hypothesis about the present or the future). The suffix -ydi moves the hypothesis into the past.

quiz.why: -seydi is a past conditional: if you had come.
keşke expresses regret or a wish: if only.

items.title: Passive and causative
items.goal: Say « it is done », « I had it done » and understand verbs in -ıl / -dır.

blocks.text: The passive is formed with -ıl / -il / -ul / -ül after a consonant, and -n after a vowel: yazmak → yazılmak (to be written), okumak → okunmak (to be read), yapmak → yapılmak (to be done), görmek → görülmek (to be seen).

The causative means « to have something done » or « to let something happen ». Add -dır / -dir / -tır / -tir (or -t, -ir, -er) depending on the verb and its final consonant: yapmak → yaptırmak (to have done), okumak → okutmak (to have read), yazmak → yazdırmak (to have written), temizlemek → temizletmek (to have cleaned).

blocks.caption: The four forms of yapmak
head: Form
Turkish
Meaning
rows: someone had it done / I was made to do it

blocks.text: <tur>gelmek → getirmek</tur> (to bring, to make come), <tur>gitmek → götürmek</tur> (to take away, to make go), <tur>görmek → göstermek</tur> (to show). These forms are lexicalised: learn them as separate verbs.

The agent is expressed with <tur>tarafından</tur>: <tur>Bu roman, genç bir yazar tarafından yazılmış.</tur> (This novel was written by a young author.) The passive is widely used in formal texts, instructions and news reports.

items.fr: This book was written in 1990.
I had a house built for myself.
The teacher made us read the text.
He was taken to Ankara.

blocks.text: Suffixes can chain together: <tur>yap-tır-ıl-mak</tur> (to be made to be done). In a sentence, look first at the last suffix: it tells you whether the action is passive, causative or both.

quiz.why: The causative -dır indicates that you have the action done by someone else.
yazıldı is the passive of yazmak: it was written.
